clips.title: Temporal 101: Build Your First Durable Application
clips.why: A quick reminder of what a Temporal run is before we start naming runs: Temporal records every step, so a run can sleep, crash or wait for a signal and carry on.
look: Every step of a run is recorded, which is why a run is a real, long-lived thing worth giving a proper name.
He mentions waiting for an external signal: that is how a second trigger can talk to a run that is already open.
The AI agent loop example: the agent's history survives because Temporal brings the run back in the same state.
clips.after: Nova's run for a ticket lives for minutes or hours and holds a VM, so starting a second one by accident is expensive, and that is what this lesson prevents.
clips.quote: we pick up exactly where it left off

clips.title: Temporal Explained • Idempotence
clips.why: Inserting a row with an auto-generated key twice gives two rows, which is exactly what random workflow IDs do to runs; the fix is a key that recognises the repeat.
look: The auto-generated primary key example: same values, new key each time, so two records. Swap 'record' for 'run' and 'key' for 'random workflow ID'.
'Idempotent or its effects are de-duplicated': a meaningful workflow ID is how we de-duplicate starts.
The definition of an idempotency key: a unique value that lets the receiver recognise a repeated request.
clips.after: nova:RH-1234 is our idempotency key for starting work: every trigger for the ticket carries the same key, so Temporal recognises the repeat instead of creating a second run.
clips.quote: An idempotency key is a unique value

clips.title: Datadog @ Replay 2026 | 100 Temporal Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
clips.why: A Datadog engineer shows two real fixes: build a key from the workflow ID so retries match, and when a thing with the same name already exists, use it instead of failing.
look: The key is built from the workflow ID, so it stays the same on every attempt: the same idea as naming the run after the ticket.
The Kubernetes job example: creating a job with a name that already exists fails, again and again. That is our default policy, FAIL.
The fix is 'skip creation and get the status of the existing job', which is what USE_EXISTING does for a run.
clips.after: Our startRun makes the same choice for runs: a second start for nova:RH-1234 does not fail on the existing name, it joins the open run and gets a handle to it.
clips.quote: skip creation and getting the status of the existing job

practice.q: The Jira poll, Slack /nova and a Jira comment can all ask Nova to work on RH-1234. Which workflow ID makes all three land in one run?

options.why: Every call gets a new name, so Temporal sees three different jobs and starts three runs.
All three triggers build the same name, nova:RH-1234, so the second and third meet the run that is already open.
The timestamp makes every name different again. It looks meaningful, but it behaves like a random ID.

practice.q: Finish startRun so a second start for the same ticket joins the run that is already working.
practice.hint: Two words, joined by an underscore: the policy that returns a handle to the open run.
practice.why: USE_EXISTING turns a second start into 'here is the run that is already open', so Slack can reply with a link instead of an error.

practice.q: You set a fixed workflow ID but no conflict policy, and start nova:RH-1234 twice while the first run is still open. What does the second start throw?
practice.hint: It is the error the lab prints for the default policy, FAIL.
practice.why: FAIL is the default: Temporal refuses a second open run with the same ID and throws WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError. It is safe, but every caller has to handle the error.

practice.q: startRun uses `nova:${ticket}` and USE_EXISTING. Put what happens on a busy morning in order.
items: The Jira poll calls startRun for RH-1234, no open run has the name nova:RH-1234, so Temporal starts one
The run claims one of Nova's three VM slots and starts reading the code
You type /nova RH-1234 in Slack, Temporal finds nova:RH-1234 open and returns a handle to it
Slack replies with a link to the run that is already working
A minute later the poll asks again and gets a handle to the same run, so there is still one run and one VM
practice.why: Only the first start creates anything. Every later trigger for the same name joins the open run, so the number of runs stays at one however often people ask.

practice.q: Yesterday the run nova:RH-1234 finished. Today the ticket is assigned to Nova again and the poll calls startRun. You did not set a reuse policy. What happens?

options.text: A brand new run starts with the same ID, nova:RH-1234
options.why: The one-run-per-name rule only covers open runs. The default reuse policy, ALLOW_DUPLICATE, lets a closed name be used again, so the ticket gets a fresh run and a fresh VM.

options.text: The poll gets a handle to yesterday's finished run
options.why: USE_EXISTING only joins a run that is still open. A finished run cannot be joined.
That only happens while the old run is open, or if you chose REJECT_DUPLICATE, which refuses names that were used before.

practice.q: Main breaks, and every new red build carries more evidence about the same problem. The CI fixer's run for this root cause may or may not be open yet. Which call fits?

options.why: One call: if the run is open it gets the signal with the new build's details, and if not, Temporal starts it and then delivers the signal. One run, and no evidence lost.
You would get one run, but the new build's details stay with the caller. Joining the run does not hand it a message.
Every red build would kill the fixer's work in progress and start again from zero. A second trigger should never destroy work.
